paper.title: Coordinated Reply Attacks in Influence Operations: Characterization and Detection
paper.venue: Proceedings of the Nineteenth International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2025)
paper.version: AAAI/ICWSM official PDF; arXiv 2410.19272 cross-checked as preprint source
paper.page_convention: 1-based PDF page numbers; PDF p.1 is printed page 1586

text_evidence_sources: official GitHub README and API metadata

claims.claim: Coordinated reply attacks in the studied Twitter IO data primarily target influential public figures such as journalists, news media, state officials, and politicians.

evidence.note: Target account and tweet/reply distribution CCDFs.
Serbia target country/profession and word-shift case study.
Egypt target country/profession and word-shift case study.
Manual annotation and case-study conclusions.

caveats: The target-profile annotation is limited to Serbia and Egypt case studies and was performed by one author.
The paper explicitly says the descriptive statistics lack a general Twitter-user reference model.

claims.claim: A supervised tweet classifier can identify tweets targeted by coordinated replies within the constructed dataset.

evidence.note: Positive/control tweet construction.
Random Forest F1 0.80 and AUC 0.88.
All features outperform simple tweet-level counts.
Permutation importance for tweet classifier.
Threshold robustness from 5 to 20 IO replies.

caveats: The claim depends on the paper's positive and control construction.
The tweet dataset is artificially balanced.

claims.claim: A supervised replier classifier can identify IO repliers among replies to targeted tweets in the studied data.

evidence.note: Downsampling plus Random Forest F1 0.92 and AUC 0.97.
Similarity features are the strongest single feature set.
Similarity dominates permutation importance.
IO replies have higher similarity distribution than normal replies.
Performance under different class imbalance ratios.

caveats: The strongest table result is from balanced downsampling, not an online prevalence setting.
IO replier label should not be interpreted as harmful intent.

claims.claim: The classifiers show partial cross-campaign generalization within Twitter IO campaigns.

evidence.note: Tweet classifier cross-campaign F1 matrix has uneven off-diagonal drops.
Replier classifier cross-campaign F1 matrix is stronger but still has weak campaign pairs.

caveats: All cross-campaign tests remain inside the Twitter IO data universe.
The paper does not evaluate on other platforms due to lack of IO datasets.

claims.claim: Reply-level engagement and similarity are important operational signals for coordinated reply detection.

evidence.note: Engagement feature set improves tweet classifier over simple counts.
Tweet-level feature importance emphasizes reply-level engagement.
Similarity feature set reaches F1 0.84 and AUC 0.92 for replier classifier.
Similarity dominates replier importance and has visible distributional separation.

caveats: Similarity can arise from common topic or event context, not only malicious coordination.
Permutation importance is not a causal test.

claims.claim: For CogGuard, the paper supports tactic-specific reply-attack detection, not direct community harmfulness labeling.

evidence.note: Authors discuss safety impact and warn that activism may also use coordinated replies.
Authors recommend human investigation and warn against labeling users as IO accounts without thorough investigation.
Labels are based on Twitter IO membership and reply timing, not harmful intent annotation.

caveats: This is a migration recommendation by the report, not a direct paper claim.
IO membership, coordination, and harmful intent are distinct constructs.
